items.title: [Spec & Ecosystem] Lack of enforced Server-level routing descriptions breaks LLM tool selection under Lazy/Deferred Loading (especially when paired with Agent Skills)
items.author: gavincrossv1
items.body: ### What's broken? The spec doesn't cover a case it clearly should ### Where in the spec or docs? https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/basic/lifecycle#initialization , https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/server/tools , and schema.ts (InitializeResult / Implementation) ### What should happen? The MCP specification and documentation should explicitly address **Lazy / Deferred Tool Loading** (where hosts do not inject full `Tool` schemas into the initial LLM context to avoid token bloat) and define clear requirements for **first-level server routing metadata**: 1. **In the Lifecycle / Initialization & Tools Spec**: Clarify that while individual `Tool.description` fields describe atomic operations, **`InitializeResult.serverInfo.description` (or a concise routing summary in `InitializeResult.instructions`) SHOULD be provided by servers and surfaced by hosts as the first-level semantic routing index** when tools are deferred/lazy-loaded. 2. **Host Implementation Guidance**: When a host implements lazy tool loading (e.g., listing available MCP servers in the system prompt or inside a `ToolSearch` meta-tool and deferring `.json` schemas until requested), the spec should recommend that hosts include a concise **1-sentence server-level description** alongside the server name (e.g., `# playwright: Browser automation server for navigating pages, clicking elements, and capturing accessibility snapshots`), rather than stripping the representation down to bare identifiers only. *(Note: A typical workspace mounts only 1–5 MCP servers, so surfacing a 30-word server summary costs <150 tokens total while preserving semantic routing accuracy.)* 3. **SDK Alignment**: Official SDKs (such as Python `FastMCP` and the TypeScript SDK) should encourage providing a concise server `description` upon initialization (or fall back to extracting the module docstring) so that servers in the ecosystem actually populate `serverInfo.description`. ### What actually happens? ### 1. Spec & Schema Reality Historically, the MCP specification assumed **Eager Loading** (hosts injecting all `Tool` definitions from `tools/list` directly into the LLM's `tools` array). Therefore: - Semantic descriptions were bound strictly to individual tools (`Tool.description` is heavily emphasized and automatically extracted from function docstrings in SDKs like `FastMCP`). - At the server level (`InitializeResult.serverInfo` / `Implementation`), only `name` and `version` are required: ```typescript export interface Implementation extends BaseMetadata, Icons { version: string; description?: string; // Optional human-readable description, rarely populated in practice } ``` - Because `serverInfo.description` is optional and framed as human/UI metadata rather than an LLM routing index, almost all MCP servers in the wild (including `@playwright/mcp`) only return `name` and `version`: ```python # Standard FastMCP pattern in the ecosystem: no server-level description mcp = FastMCP("playwright") ``` ### 2. What Breaks in Practice Under Lazy Loading To prevent 20–50 tool schemas per server from exhausting the context window, modern Agent hosts (e.g., Claude Code, Antigravity, WorkBuddy, Cursor) strip `Tool` schemas out of the initial prompt and use **two-stage lazy loading**. Once `Tool.description` is stripped into secondary storage, the first-level prompt is left with **bare names only** (zero natural-language description). When an Agent environment simultaneously uses **Agent Skills** (`SKILL.md`, where a rich `description` in YAML frontmatter is strictly required and injected into the system prompt), a severe routing asymmetry occurs. Below is an actual comparison from production Agent system prompts when both `@playwright/mcp` and an open-source browser skill (`vercel-labs/agent-browser`) are installed: **Lazy MCP in System Prompt (Zero Description):** ```xml For lazily-loaded tools, read the corresponding schema file to understand the arguments and usage, then call the tool using the `call_mcp_tool` tool. # playwright Lazy: browser_close, browser_navigate, browser_click, browser_type, browser_snapshot, ... mcp__playwright ``` **Skills in the Same System Prompt (Rich Description + `MUST` Directive):** ```xml If a skill seems relevant to your current task, you MUST read its `SKILL.md` instructions using `view_file` before proceeding. Available skills: - agent-browser (.../SKILL.md): Browser automation CLI for AI agents. Use when the user needs to interact with websites, including navigating pages, filling forms, clicking buttons, taking screenshots, extracting data... ``` ### 3. Reproduction & Benchmark: 2m36s (MCP) vs. 8m19s (Skill) We tested the following task in an environment with both `playwright` MCP and `agent-browser` Skill installed: > *"Open the Tianjin University homepage (https://www.tju.edu.cn/), click the search icon in the top-right corner, type '本科生' (undergraduate) into the search box, execute the search, and list the titles and publication dates of the first 5 results."* - **Case 1: Without specifying the tool (Natural Routing — Broken)**: Because `playwright` MCP has no description in the first-level index while `agent-browser` has a keyword-rich description paired with a `MUST` rule, the LLM immediately chooses the `agent-browser` Skill on turn 1. Once the multi-hundred-line `SKILL.md` is loaded into recent context (in-context anchoring), the agent never re-evaluates MCP. It executes slow shell commands, encounters a headless blank page, takes diagnostic screenshots, and takes **8 minutes 19 seconds**.

items.title: mcp: a caller cannot detect that a provider's tool definitions changed
items.author: HosniBelfeki
items.body:
## The gap

A caller that reaches a provider over `/sam/mcp/1.0.0` verifies **who** the provider is — the Biscuit is signed by a trusted control-plane key, bound to the peer, unexpired, carrying `sam:role:node`. Nothing verifies that the tool it is about to call is the same tool it saw last time.

The mesh deliberately takes the live value as authoritative. `verifyGossipToolRows` (`internal/node/mcp_handlers.go:344`):

> *treats unsolicited announcements as routing hints, not authorization evidence. Each candidate is confirmed through the existing authenticated MCP session and exact tools/list response before it is exposed.*

and `verifyGossipToolRowsWithFetcher` keeps the fetched description, discarding what was announced. That is correct for an announcement, and it also means nothing in the mesh remembers what a tool looked like before.

The control plane does not fill that role: `NodeCatalogReport` (`api/sam.proto:367`) is *"Display-only; carries no authorization weight."*

An enrolled node can therefore change a tool's description or its input schema at any time, and every caller keeps treating it as the tool it originally reviewed.

## Why it matters

This is a named class — "MCP rug pull". The Cloud Security Alliance describes it as *"tool definitions changed server-side after security review and user approval"*, with the impact *"persistent covert access after trust has been established; compliance audit failure"*. Invariant Labs published it as a security notification.

The MCP specification's security best practices (2026-07-28) names nine threats; this is not among them. A mesh that wants to address it is on its own.

## Enrolled providers

SAM providers hold a control-plane credential rather than being arbitrary servers someone installed, which narrows the threat but does not remove it. Enrollment proves identity, not intent, and a compromised but still-enrolled node is the case `AGENTS.md` names:

> *Zero Trust: Assume no implicit trust between nodes, control planes, routers, or external actors.*

The trust a caller places in a tool definition is currently implicit, and it is the one input to the agent's decision that nothing in the mesh attests.

## Sketch

Modelled on `required_labels`, so it lands where callers already look:

1. A canonical digest over the `tools/list` response — tool names, descriptions, input and output schemas, deterministically ordered and serialised.
2. An optional `expected_tools_digest` on the session, alongside `required_labels`.
3. A mismatch refuses the session with a typed error, as `LabelsNotSatisfiedError` does.
4. All three implementations, to keep the SDK parity matrix accurate.

## Open questions

- **Opt-in or default?** Tools legitimately change, and MCP has `tools/list_changed`. A caller-supplied pin seems right; a mesh-wide default does not.
- **Where does the first digest come from?** Trust on first use, or operator configuration. The second is stronger and needs a configuration path.
- **Canonicalisation.** JSON Schema has map ordering and number formatting; a digest that is not byte-stable produces false alarms. Getting this wrong is worse than not having it.

## Limits

This detects change, not malice. A provider hostile from the first call is unaffected — it is a continuity control, not a trust decision.

Happy to implement whichever shape you settle on, or to drop it if continuity belongs elsewhere in the design.

items.title: Docs: quickstart MCP configs use unpinned `npx -y`, contradicting the Local Server Security guide
items.author: basitalisandhu
items.body:
### What's broken?

The documentation is wrong or misleading

### Where in the spec or docs?

https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/develop/connect-local-servers and https://modelcontextprotocol.io/examples

### What should happen?

The beginner examples should follow the [Local Server Security](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/tutorials/security/local-server-security) guide, which says to "Install a specific version rather than `latest`". For example `"args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem@1.0.0", ...]`, plus one sentence linking to that guide.

### What actually happens?

The pages people copy from start every server unpinned: `docs/develop/connect-local-servers.mdx` (lines 100, 116, 216, 220, 273), `docs/examples.mdx` (lines 43, 50, 66 to 78), `docs/develop/build-client.mdx` (961) and `docs/tools/debugging.mdx` (131), in both the 2026-07-28 and draft versions. Each launch can fetch whatever was published last.

The pattern is widespread. In a random sample of 2,999 public GitHub repositories that ship agent skills or MCP configs, 159 of the 346 repositories that configure a local MCP server (46.0%) start at least one with no pinned version, and 63 of 346 (18.2%) ask for `latest` outright. A hand check found 19 of 22 findings correct. Caveat: it is a sample of what GitHub code search surfaces, not a census. Data and method: https://github.com/basitalisandhu/agent-skills-state-2026

### Anything else?

The registry already rejects `latest` and version ranges for `server.json` packages (`internal/validators/validators.go`), so these docs are the main place that still teaches the unpinned form. If maintainers agree, I am happy to open the docs PR.

AI disclosure: I used Claude Code to help prepare the analysis and draft this issue.

items.title: M30.4 · Signed snapshot manifest + verification (unified cloud/local trust root) [P1]
items.author: nebuk89
items.body:
**Priority: P1** (trust model; cross-repo with gctl). Part of **M30**; see `docs/security-model.md` invariants I6 + finding §3 M30.4 / M30.7 (unified trust root).

### Finding (security review)
Snapshot trust is missing — bundle contents and `state.json` are trusted; and app/cloud signing consistency is needed (one trust model).

### Verified against the code
- `materialize_bundle` verifies each object against `manifest.checksum_tree` (integrity — detects corruption) but there is **no signature** (authenticity — nothing proves the manifest itself came from the cloud). A tampered bundle with a recomputed `checksum_tree` passes.

### Plan (cross-repo with gimbal-cloud-control)
- [ ] **Signed manifest**: the manifest hashes every file **plus** runtime metadata (substrate, gic_mode, origin, sizes) and carries a **signature** over that manifest, produced by the cloud/capture signing key.
- [ ] `chm` (and the app before it exposes "Run") **verify the signature** against a trusted public key, then verify `checksum_tree`, then record provenance.
- [ ] **One trust root**: the app trusts the cloud/capture public keys; gctl signs manifests; Gimbal Local verifies + records provenance before exposing "Run". Makes M26's displayed provenance (`source_kind` / `origin_substrate`) cryptographically verified.

### Boundary
gctl owns producing + signing the manifest (needs the signing contract, like M27/M28 track their contracts); Gimbal Local owns verification. Blocked on the gctl manifest-signing spec.


## Sizing (2026-09-10)

**size/L — 5–10 person-days; medium confidence; deliverable.**
Planning estimate, not measured duration (one familiar engineer).

Remaining is integration/acceptance, not rebuilding Ed25519 verification or a missing plane signer. gimbal-dev/gimbal-cloud-control#1 closed with v0.11.0 signing/JWKS evidence. Its published embedded base64/kid contract differs from local raw-byte detached hex/key_id expectations; live interoperability was not measured here. First slice: 1–2 days comparing a real signed assignment/key fixture and agreeing the contract. Range covers needed adaptation, trusted key rotation/revocation, fail-closed/provenance paths and joint negative/hardware acceptance. Requires CP coordination and trust-bootstrap decisions, excluding waiting. #39 contains this effort; #20/#21 and future #159 reuse parts. Existing blocked label is preserved, not treated as proof that the producer is unbuilt.

_Basis: `2026-07-15T12:12:10Z` + all comments._

items.title: rmoriebricklayer 0.5.8: third review, fixed at every sibling
items.author: rootcoder007
items.body:
Third review of the hardening work (`rmoriebricklayer_0.5.7_stress_2026-10-06.md`): seven findings, each a fix that had landed at one site and not its siblings. This branch fixes every one at every site of its kind and puts the sibling enumeration into the tests (`test-review3.R`, `test-src-hygiene.R`) so a new site cannot appear unnoticed.

**N1 (HIGH)** `bricklayer_siu_text()` / `bricklayer_parse_siu()` killed R on 25 KB of whitespace: libstdc++ regex recursion, not catchable. Every whole-document pass is a loop now, byte-identical to the regexes it replaced (the test keeps the old pipeline as an R reference); every line the extractors see is capped at 4,000 characters; every SIU entry caps input at 2 MiB; a subprocess battery runs ten hostile inputs through every one-string SIU entry enumerated from the namespace. Same fix and guard ported to rmorie and morie, which vendor the core.

**N2 (HIGH)** `manifest_canonical` is one-to-one: the names attribute decides object vs array at every level, empty names included; a named atomic vector is an object. One attestation no longer verifies two documents.

**N3** Every network byte goes through `src/rmbl_fetch.cpp`: `bricklayer_download()` (progress bar via a libcurl callback), `download_data()`, `bricklayer_json_from_json()`. The transport drops credential headers on a cross-host redirect, refuses https→http, validates before opening the destination and never deletes a pre-existing file; the redirect rule is a pure function with its own `.Call` and tests; single-label hostnames refused by shape. A hygiene test lists every network open in `R/`.

**N4** Barrier clears the interrupt flag on entry and every exit; a kernel called with no barrier active re-raises the interrupt; `rmbl_pbkdf2_sha256()` returns int. **N5** identifier heuristic needs 100 rows a side. **N6/N7** `log_p_value` on `mahalanobis_outliers()`, documented everywhere; `drift_psi(eps)` accepts (0, 1) again with the floor explained. Also: bounded Mann-Kendall memo, underscore hostnames, `Makevars.win` fallback wired, `rmbl_digest_equal()` barrier, XMSS interrupt site.

Reviewer suites: 0.5.5 → 41/0; 0.5.6 → 35 behaved (3 known artefacts); 0.5.7 → 27 behaved, 1 remaining item is a hard-coded `chk(..., FALSE)` in the reproducer.

items.title: harden-tenant-provisioning: Phase B2 — per-tenant runtime state, readiness gate, bootstrap hardening
items.author: kikokikok
items.body:
Tracking issue for **Phase B2** of `openspec/changes/harden-tenant-provisioning` (groups 5 and 6 in `tasks.md`), plus carry-over items from Phase B1 not covered by the `SecretBackend` stack (#94/#95/#96/#98).

## Scope

### Carry-over from Phase B1 (manifest schema + hashing)

Not delivered by #94–#96. These are prerequisite for most B2 work because the readiness gate keys off the manifest's `providers` block.

- [ ] 1.1 Extend `TenantManifest` with `metadata.generation: u64` and `providers: ManifestProviders` (memoryLayers, llm, embedding). `cli/src/server/tenant_api.rs:3404`
- [ ] 1.3 Create `manifest_canonical` module: stable key order, inline secrets stripped.
- [ ] 1.4 Implement `manifest_hash(&TenantManifest) -> String` returning `sha256:<hex>`.
- [ ] 1.5 Add `last_applied_manifest_hash: Option<String>` and `generation: u64` columns to `tenants`; write SQL migration.
- [ ] 1.6 Update `provision_tenant` (`tenant_api.rs:3599`) to compute+persist hash, enforce monotonic generation, short-circuit no-op re-applies. Rewrite `provision_tenant_idempotent_reapply` (L5674) to assert the short-circuit path.
- [ ] 1.7 Extend `validate_manifest` to cover unknown `SecretReference.kind`, invalid generation, missing required provider declarations.
- [ ] Legacy cleanup: remove `storage/src/secret_provider.rs` now that all callers use `SecretBackend`. Assert with grep in CI.

### Group 5 — Per-tenant provider state and readiness gate

Depends on the wiring-model decision in 0.2 of `tasks.md` (lazy vs eager). Design decision needs to be captured in `design.md` before implementation starts.

- [ ] 5.1 Define `TenantRuntimeState` enum `{ Loading, Available, LoadingFailed { reason } }`.
- [ ] 5.2 Implement the wiring model chosen in 0.2. If lazy: record first-resolution outcome per tenant and surface it. If eager: startup loop over persisted tenants.
- [ ] 5.3 Extend `/ready` (`cli/src/server/health.rs:40`, handler at L58) to include a tenant-state check alongside PG + vector. Return 503 until bootstrap completes AND all tenants resolved.
- [ ] 5.4 In tenant-scoped routes (`/api/v1/memory/*` and siblings), short-circuit to HTTP 503 `{error: "tenant_unavailable", tenantSlug, reason}` when target tenant is `LoadingFailed`.
- [ ] 5.5 Extend `/admin/tenants/{tenant}/providers/status` (`tenant_api.rs:2818`). Current response is `{llm, embedding}`. Add `state`, `reason`, `providersWired[]`, `providersFailed[]` (non-breaking: new optional fields).
- [ ] 5.6 Metrics: `aeterna_tenant_state{slug, state}` gauge, `aeterna_tenant_wiring_duration_seconds` histogram.

### Group 6 — First-run bootstrap hardening

- [ ] 6.1 Refactor `bootstrap.rs` to run idempotently; add `GET /api/v1/admin/bootstrap/status` returning per-step status.
- [ ] 6.2 Gate `/ready` on bootstrap completion (in concert with 5.3).
- [ ] 6.3 Structured error on failure; `/ready` stays 503; retry on pod restart.
- [ ] 6.4 Emit `BootstrapCompleted` governance event on success.

## Acceptance

- `/ready` returns 503 on fresh pod until bootstrap completes *and* every persisted tenant is in `Available` state (or explicitly excluded).
- A tenant with a broken `providers` manifest fails readiness with a structured reason exposed via `/admin/tenants/{slug}/providers/status`; the pod does not accept traffic for that tenant's routes.
- Re-applying the same manifest twice causes the second call to short-circuit (no DB writes, no audit row duplication) and is observable via `manifest_hash` equality in audit.
- An integration test kills Postgres mid-bootstrap, restarts the pod, and asserts bootstrap resumes cleanly (idempotency).
- `aeterna_tenant_state{state="loading_failed"}` fires an alert in the default rules shipped in `observability/`.

## Dependencies and decisions needed before implementation

- **0.2** (wiring model: eager vs lazy) blocks 5.2, 5.3, 5.4, 6.2.
- Eager wiring interacts with the `SecretBackend` boot path already introduced by #94. If we go eager, the startup loop needs the backend fully built *before* it runs, which already matches `build_secret_backend_from_env` at startup.
- Readiness gating must not regress the rolling-restart semantics documented in `docs/guides/ha-deployment.md`. Explicit test required.

## Out of scope (later phases)

- Phase B3 (dry-run / diff / render endpoints).
- Phase B4 (secret resolver kind-dispatch, inline-gating) — depends on 0.1.
- Phase B5 (CLI refactor `apply/render/diff/validate/watch`) — depends on 0.4.
- Phase B6 (scoped automation tokens).
- Phase B7 (audit parity, UI, docs, consistency harness).

## Related

- Design: `openspec/changes/harden-tenant-provisioning/design.md`
- Tasks: `openspec/changes/harden-tenant-provisioning/tasks.md` (groups 1, 5, 6)
- B1 docs: #98, `docs/architecture/secret-backend.md`
- B1 merged: #94 #95 #96

items.title: feat(proof): require miner hotkey signature on submit
items.author: echobt
items.body: ## Summary Mandatory miner sr25519 signature on Proof `POST /v1/submissions`. A bare 64-hex `miner_hotkey` can no longer be spoofed, a captured signature cannot be reused with another claim / FLOPs / manifest, and an identical request cannot be replayed. Architecte lock (domain `base-proof-submit-v1`, a new `crypto::DomainTag`; not a reuse of topic / bundle / rawweight): ``` payload = hotkey_hex || 0xff || topic_id || 0xff || artifact_digest || 0xff || declared_flops_decimal || 0xff || claim || 0xff || manifest_canonical || 0xff || submit_nonce_hex manifest_canonical = count(hashes)_decimal || (0xff || hash)* # train_content_hashes, sorted bytewise || 0xff || count(datasets)_decimal || (0xff || dataset)* # train_dataset_ids, sorted bytewise ``` - Wire: required `hotkey_signature` (**exactly** 128 lowercase hex, no `0x`) and `submit_nonce` (**exactly** 64 lowercase hex = 32 client-chosen random bytes). `miner_hotkey` is the 64-hex public key that must verify the signature. - Server: after parse + topic-open checks, verify **before insert**. Missing/empty sig → **401** `hotkey_signature required`; bad encoding / verify fail (incl. tampered manifest) → **401** `hotkey_signature invalid`; nonce missing / malformed → **401** `submit_nonce required` / `submit_nonce invalid`. Then `(hotkey, nonce)` is reserved atomically in the submission store **before** any budget check, rent, or row: a replay is **401** `submit_nonce reused` and never evaluates twice. No unsigned grace. Refusals leave no row. - Client: `ctx proof submit` / `ctx proof sign` sign via keystore (Substrate/sr25519), draw a fresh nonce per run, print `submit_nonce` + the exact `manifest` to post; `--submit-nonce` pins one (required with `--signature`). - Docs: gateway host + signature + nonce required; exact bytes and a Python reference in `docs/external-miner/proof.md`. - Out of scope: `X-Lium-Api-Key` is not identity. Queued / `defer_scoring` stays on its own PR. New crate `crates/proof-submit` (proof-task is at the loc-cap). `MemoryStore` gains `submit_nonce` on rows and `reserve_submit_nonce` (same durability as the rows: Proof submission state is in-memory today). ## Greptile Every PR is reviewed by Greptile before merge. Config: `.greptile/`. - [x] Greptile has reviewed this PR; findings are fixed (P1 manifest, P1 replay, P2 encoding) — re-review requested - [x] Commented `@greptileai review` ## Test plan - [x] `cargo test -p proof-submit` (payload bytes, canonical manifest injectivity, strict hex, round-trip / tamper / wrong key) - [x] `cargo test -p proof-store` (nonce reserved once per hotkey) - [x] `cargo test -p proof-http --lib` (401 rows: missing / zero / `0x` / uppercase / wrong-key sig; missing / malformed nonce; tampered manifest; identical replay → 401 + one row; reordered manifest with a fresh nonce → 201) - [x] `cargo test -p proof-http --test live_submit_e2e` - [x] `cargo test -p ctx` (secret-file signs manifest + nonce, fresh nonce per run, offline signature needs its nonce, CLI parse) - [x] `cargo test -p proof-rlm-scorer --test rlm_e2e` - [x] `cargo test -p proof-challenge-bin --test submit_e2e` - [x] `cargo clippy -p proof-submit -p proof-store -p proof-http -p ctx -p proof-rlm-scorer -p proof-challenge-bin -p xtask --all-targets -- -D warnings` - [x] `cargo fmt --all -- --check` - [x] `cargo run -p xtask -- loc-cap` · `external-docs-check` - [x] `deploy/scripts/proof-submit-sign.sh` exercised locally (fresh + pinned nonce); `proof-submit-e2e.sh --probe` replays a scored body and expects 401 `submit_nonce reused` ## Risk New cryptographic domain `base-proof-submit-v1` (additive; existing `base-*` tags unchanged). Live Proof submits without `hotkey_signature` + `submit_nonce` will 401. Miner docs, `ctx`, and operator probes updated. No `BASE_*` rename, no emission / leaf / seal change. ## Naming I did **not** rename `BASE_*` environment variables, deployed host paths (`/opt/base`, `/run/base`, …), GHCR `baseintelligence/base` package names, or `base-*-v1` cryptographic domain tags, unless this PR’s purpose is a coordinated cutover documented in `docs/NAMING.md`. This PR **adds** `base-proof-submit-v1` alongside `base-proof-topic-v1`.

items.title: Register frozen datasets: yfinance provider marked personal use, immutable dataset_versions tied to their ids
items.author: BugHunterX2101
items.body:
This PR is the second part of R1, the dataset registry. It adds the provider interface with yfinance as a `personal_use_only` source, and the registry tables in PostgreSQL. No job or endpoint uses them yet: the snapshot job and its API come in the next PR, so no behaviour changes.

## What it adds

`backend/services/dataset_providers.py`
- **Interface:** `Provider`, `SnapshotRequest` (1 to 50 symbols, a start date included and an end date excluded) and `Snapshot` (datasets, unavailable symbols, client version, retrieval time). The licence registry is `LICENCES`.
- **`YahooProvider`:**
  - It splits the requested symbols into one dataset per family: `EQUITY_EOD` (equities and ETFs), `INDEX_EOD`, `CRYPTO_SPOT_EOD`, `FX_SPOT_EOD`, `FUTURES_CONTINUOUS_EOD` and `FUND_NAV_EOD`.
  - Each dataset holds three tables: bars, corporate actions (dividends, splits, capital gains) and instruments (exchange, IANA timezone, quote currency).
  - A symbol the provider cannot describe is reported with a reason and is never guessed. This covers unknown instrument types, missing metadata, crypto not dated in UTC, timestamps that are not local midnights, duplicate sessions and yfinance errors. The other symbols in the request are unaffected.

`backend/services/dataset_format.py`: adds the `INSTRUMENTS_V1` schema, and corrects the bars comment, which said bars are always raw.

Migration `0004` and `backend/services/dataset_registry.py`
- **`dataset_versions`:** one row per verified blob, holding:
  - identity, licence flags, `point_in_time`, coverage and symbols;
  - the canonical manifest and per-table manifests;
  - blob format, SHA-256 and size;
  - provenance: the request, the client version and the retrieval time.
- **Immutability:**
  - Grants: the app and worker roles get SELECT and INSERT only.
  - A row trigger refuses UPDATE and DELETE, even for the owner.
  - A statement trigger refuses TRUNCATE.
- **CHECKs:**
  - `dataset_id` must equal `'qs-ds-sha256-v1:' || encode(sha256(manifest_canonical), 'hex')`.
  - The identity columns must equal the identity inside that manifest.
  - So a writer that computes the id wrongly, or labels a split-adjusted dataset as raw, fails the insert.
- **`user_datasets`:** records who fetched which dataset. Personal-use data is listed only to the users who fetched it.
- **`register()`:** derives every field from a dataset that was already read back and verified from the store. Registering the same content again keeps the first row; a different blob under an existing id is refused.

## Decisions, and the evidence for them

These were measured with yfinance 1.5.2 on 2026-10-11:

- **Yahoo serves no raw prices, so the identity says `adjustment: split`.** AAPL's close on 2020-08-28 comes back as 124.8075, and volume as 187.6M. Those are the actual $499.23 print / 4 and the actual 46.9M shares × 4. That holds over ten years each of AAPL, MSFT, SPY, KO and T, with 40 dividends each. So the next PRs can keep the tasks' current split-and-dividend-adjusted inputs.
- **Session dates are local.** Daily bars come dated at local midnight in the exchange's timezone. The session date is that local date: a Tokyo bar is not moved to the previous UTC day.

items.title: M30.4: Ed25519 signed-manifest verification + reference signer (chm side)
items.author: nebuk89
items.body:
## Why

M30.4 is the biggest missing trust feature: bundle **integrity** (does it match its manifest?) was enforced by re-hashing against `checksum_tree`, but **authenticity** (did the manifest come from a trusted signer?) was not — a tampered bundle whose `checksum_tree` was recomputed to match passed. This ships the verification half (the boundary we own); gctl owns producing+signing production manifests (#36 remains open for that cross-repo half).

No new dependencies: Ed25519 via the already-vendored `ring`.

## What changed

**Signing module + CLI (`signing.rs`).** Ed25519 sign/verify, a hex codec, a detached-signature envelope (`{alg,key_id,sig}`), and a `TrustStore` mapping `key_id -> public key` (so keys rotate). The signature covers the manifest's raw bytes, so signer and verifier need not agree on a canonical JSON encoding. `chm manifest keygen|sign|verify` is a local signer that is both the end-to-end test vehicle and gctl's reference implementation.

**Ingest gate (`control_plane.rs`).** Both ingest paths (assign-run and pull) now run an authenticity gate. With a trust root configured (`CHM_TRUST_STORE`), the assignment must carry `manifest_canonical` + `manifest_signature`; the signature is verified and the **signed** manifest's `checksum_tree` is used (never the loose one). Missing/invalid signature **fails closed**. Without a trust root, the unsigned tree is used so pre-signing flows keep working during rollout.

## Verification

99 chm tests (added 8 signing + 4 gate tests: sign/verify roundtrip, tampered payload, wrong key, unknown key id, unsupported alg, bad-length key; and unsigned-allowed / fail-closed-when-trust-set / verified-uses-signed-tree / tampered-rejected). Clippy clean. The CLI was exercised end to end (keygen -> sign -> verify OK; tampered manifest -> exit 1).

## Contract for gctl

Documented in `docs/security-model.md` M30.4 and on #36: Ed25519 over the raw manifest bytes; assignment fields `manifest_canonical` (exact signed bytes) + `manifest_signature`; trust store `{ "keys": { "<id>": "<hex>" } }` via `CHM_TRUST_STORE`; key-id rotation; fail-closed. #36 stays open for gctl's signing side.

Relates to #36

items.title: Hash on-chain values in-repo; route symbol-first scans to the analyzer
items.author: metafrogmeme-droid
items.body:
Two independent fixes, both of the same species: a value that was **the correct shape and the wrong content**, with nothing in any response able to tell them apart.

---

## 1. The ERC-8257 registration plan was serving SHA-256 as `manifest_hash`

`/api/tool/registration-plan` returned:

```
manifest_hash : 0x848ee4da2d488d6ad2d3a20b6568f62a73e5b84e9c93feaa484c979b3f033a97
```

That is plain SHA-256 of the canonical manifest. The true keccak256 of the same 3324 bytes is `0x7fe3e5ecbf1d4e566d5670d99e78264d1740bd0b025198bcc086c3067737b053`. Had `registerTool` been sent, the wrong value would have been written to Base **permanently**, and no ERC-8257 verifier could ever have reproduced it.

### Why every test passed while this was broken

Production resolves `ethers` to a stub. Its `keccak256` was backed by Node's `crypto` — which has no keccak256 at all (`createHash('keccak256')` throws *Digest method not supported*) — so it fell through to SHA-256. Its `Interface.encodeFunctionData` returned the string `'0x'`.

The existing test asserted:

```js
t8257.manifestHash(m) === ethers.keccak256(ethers.toUtf8Bytes(jcs(m)))
```

Both sides are `ethers`. On the build machine that is the real package, so the assertion was a tautology in CI and absent where it mattered. This is the #999 shape one level up: the code was present and correct; production ran something else. A dependency the tests resolve differently from production is a dependency the tests do not test.

### The fix — remove what a stub can substitute

| file | what it is |
|---|---|
| `app/lib/keccak256.js` | Keccak-f[1600], 32-bit lane halves. No BigInt, no `crypto`, no npm. |
| `app/lib/abi_call.js` | Head/tail encoder for the five types these calls use. |

Known-answer vectors run before the first hash and **throw** on mismatch rather than answering with whatever the code does. That guard earned itself immediately: the first draft of `keccak256.js` carried two invented placeholder digests and it refused to hash until they were replaced with cross-checked values.

`abi_call` refuses unsupported types instead of encoding them approximately — a partial encoder that guessed would be the original bug with extra steps.

### `'0x'` calldata is not equally bad everywhere

Three call sites hand a transaction to a user's wallet:

- `tool8257.js` `registerTool` — gas spent, nothing registered
- `nft.js` `mint` — gas spent, nothing minted
- `allowances.js` `approve(spender, 0)` — **the revoke.** The user is shown "revoke this approval", their wallet confirms a real transaction, the explorer reports success, and the spender's unlimited allowance is untouched. A safety control reporting success while doing nothing.

All three now encode in-repo. In `allowances.js` the calldata is built **outside** the per-pair `try`, because inside it a broken encoder would be swallowed by `catch { unreadable++ }` and every live approval would vanish from the findings — a wallet full of unlimited grants rendering as nothing to see.

### Honesty of the plan payload

- `manifest_canonical` — the exact preimage, so the hash is checkable **without trusting this server**. That check is precisely what nobody could run while this was broken.
- `hash_algorithm` — names keccak256 and explicitly rules out SHA-256 and SHA3-256.
- Hashing and encoding are caught **separately**; a failure yields `null` plus an instruction not to register, never a placeholder that reads like the working case.

### Verification

- 601 input lengths (0–600 bytes, sweeping the 136-byte rate boundary) match real `ethers` byte for byte.
- Every wallet-facing signature matches `ethers`, including multi-byte UTF-8 and word-boundary edges.
- The live manifest now hashes to `0x7fe3e5ec…b053`.
- `app/test/ethers_stub_calldata.test.js` **installs the production stub** and drives all three paths through it. It asserts the stub is actually in place first — a reproduction that silently fails to reproduce reports the bug as fixed while exercising code that was never broken.
- Mutation-tested: reverting each of the four fixes fails exactly the test named for it.

---

## 2. "BTC scan" reached the chat model and it invented a price

The widget's quick action sends symbol-first text. The router only knew verb-first (`scan BTC`), so the message matched no rule, fell through to freeform chat, and the model published a complete *"BTC/USDT Scan — Full Analysis"* around an invented $93.06. The same fall-through produced the fabricated elliott-wave read on Telegram — both surfaces share `classify_rules`.

**The route is the grounding.** A scan reaching `analyze_asset` is built from live indicators; one reaching the chat model is fiction in the format of a measurement.

`_extract_symbol` was already correct — it resolved `BTC/USDT` from "BTC scan" the whole time. Only the rule was missing, so the rule **asks it** rather than re-deciding what a ticker looks like. Two details are load-bearing:

- **The match excludes the leading word**, so `_names_a_non_asset` gets to rule on it. `portfolio scan` keeps reaching `get_portfolio`; `wallet scan`, `technical analysis`, `risk analysis` keep falling through to chat. A first draft used a denylist in the pattern and turned all of them into analyses of `PORTFOLIO/USDT`, `WALLET/USDT`, `TECHNICAL/USDT` — the fabrication defect one level up, wearing its own fix as a costume. A denylist cannot win that race: the excluded set is every English noun, the admitted set is tickers.
- **It is registered last**, so specific intents win first. A test caught the rule taking *"close my BTC position after the scan"*: the symbol resolves there, so the `if symbol:` branch fires before `_names_a_non_asset` is consulted, and a close request became an analysis at confidence 1.0.

`analysis` joins `_CMD_WORDS` so an unlisted all-caps ticker works in both orders — `scan HYPE` already did, `HYPE analysis` did not.

# Phase C — Manifest validator + normalizer + OCI discovery

Implements the connector-manifest discovery pipeline as three coordinated modules under `src/services/connector-service/src/custos_connector/manifest/`.

## Summary

This is the next phase of the connector-service rollout, following Phase B (#321). It introduces everything the catalog gate needs to consume a connector image: validate its manifest against a stable schema, canonicalise it for content-addressing, and locate it in an OCI registry given only the subject image's digest.

## Scope

| Ticket | Module | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| #288 (CONN-IMPL-005) | `manifest/validator.py` + `manifest/_schemas/connector-manifest.v1.schema.json` | Schema-gate the v1 manifest envelope with `jsonschema` Draft 2020-12, then run typed post-checks for semver, target-config required fields, authentication-type membership, capability/event token shapes, and event delivery modes. Errors come back with a stable `ValidationErrorCode` enum and JSON-Pointer paths. |
| #289 (CONN-IMPL-006) | `manifest/normalizer.py` | Canonical JSON encoder (recursive key-sort over objects; list order preserved; tight `(",", ":")` separators; UTF-8 without escape) → SHA-256 over the resulting bytes → `sha256:<hex>` (OCI digest format). |
| #290 (CONN-IMPL-007) | `manifest/discovery.py` | Async OCI client using Distribution Spec v1.1+ Referrers API with deterministic fallback tag scheme `custos-connector-manifest-v1_sha256-<hex>`. Audit events `connector.manifest.fallback-{used,ignored,rejected}` wired through `custos_connector.audit`. |

A drift guard (`tests/test_manifest_schema_drift.py`) pins the packaged schema bytes-equal to the design source-of-truth at `design/components/connector-service/schemas/connector-manifest.v1.schema.json`.

## Tests

* **65 new unit tests** (24 validator + 15 normalizer + 25 discovery + 1 drift guard) bringing the suite to **106 passed, 97.7% coverage** (above the 90% gate; validator 91.8%, discovery 99.1%, normalizer + errors + manifest `__init__` 100%).
* **Bytes-exact fixture vectors** under `tests/fixtures/manifest_canonical/` for two real examples (`oci-registry-akv-secrets`, `amazon-s3-bucket-kms`) so any change to the canonical encoder must update both `*.canonical.json` and `*.digest.txt`.
* **Hypothesis property tests**: permutation invariance, added-field sensitivity, changed-value sensitivity (75 examples each).
* **httpx.MockTransport unit tests** for the discovery client cover the full matrix: Referrers wins (fallback-ignored audit), Referrers empty → fallback used (fallback-used audit), both empty → `NO_MANIFEST_FOUND` (rejected audit), Referrers > 1 → `AMBIGUOUS_MANIFEST` (rejected audit), malformed digest fast-fails (rejected audit), plus all transport-layer failure modes (404/4xx/5xx/network-error/non-JSON/non-object).
* **Integration tests** in `tests/integration/test_oci_discovery.py` push real images and connector-manifest artifacts against live registries and exercise both the Referrers and fallback-tag paths end-to-end.

## CI

New `connector-service-oci-integration` job attaches **both** `registry:2.8.3` and `ghcr.io/project-zot/zot-linux-amd64:v2.1.2` as service containers and runs `pytest -m oci_integration` against each. The integration fixture is parameterised by env var (`CUSTOS_OCI_REGISTRY_DISTRIBUTION_URL`, `CUSTOS_OCI_REGISTRY_ZOT_URL`) so operators can point the same suite at any conformant registry locally; if neither var is set, the fixture falls back to `testcontainers` (or skips when Docker is unavailable).

The existing `connector-service-integration` job has been scoped to `-m "integration and not oci_integration"` so the two integration shards stay independent.

## Notes

* `.gitignore`: the legacy `MANIFEST` pattern (Python sdist artifact) was also matching our new `manifest/` package directory. Pinned to a root-only `/MANIFEST` so it no longer shadows package paths.
* `pyproject.toml`: removed the `[tool.hatch.build.targets.wheel.force-include]` block that was shadowing the editable install — the in-tree schema under `src/custos_connector/manifest/_schemas/` is now picked up automatically via the existing `packages = ["src/custos_connector"]` entry.
* The canonical encoder is currently inlined in `manifest/normalizer.py` with a `TODO` to lift it to `custos-common` once that library is bootstrapped (today `custos-common` contains only a `.gitkeep`).
* Validator coverage of 91.8% reflects 7 post-schema check raise-bodies that the jsonschema gate consistently catches first (they exist for stable error codes and forward-compatibility if the schema is ever loosened). All seven are tested via the schema-gate path; the bodies themselves are pinned defensively. Coverage gate is met.

items.title: feat(execution): bind input bytes to managed execution receipts
items.author: shishenshashen
items.body:
## Summary

A managed execution receipt recorded *what* was run but not the exact bytes that were run, so two runs of the same operation key with different script bytes were indistinguishable, and a receipt registered without inputs could later be re-registered with inputs under the same key without complaint.

This PR binds the input bytes to the receipt: it records a digest per input, and it refuses a registration whose inputs differ from the recorded ones - with a named `SourceConflict` instead of the generic "operation key belongs to different work, branch or intent" message.

## What it records

- `ExecutionInput` (`awr-core/src/execution.rs`): the path as written, size, sha256, mtime and the source of the declaration (`declared` or `argv_script`). A lexically normalized form is computed by `normalized_path()` only while two inputs are compared; it is never stored.
- `ExecutionIntent.inputs` and `input_binding`, both `#[serde(default)]`, so receipts written before this change decode as "no inputs, binding `none`" instead of failing.
- `InputBinding` defaults to `None`, and both enums are `rename_all = "snake_case"`.

## Equality and the upgrade boundary

`ExecutionInput` has a handwritten `PartialEq` that leaves `mtime_ns` out and compares the normalized path, so touching a file does not make it a different input, while rewriting its bytes does. Normalization is lexical only - `a.py` equals `./a.py`, but `a.py` does not equal `dir/a.py`; it never touches the filesystem, never resolves `..`, and never folds case.

Registration compares the recorded inputs and the submitted ones after clearing both `inputs` and `input_binding` on both sides, which is what catches a receipt that was recorded with no inputs at all and is now registered with `--bind`: that case is "no inputs recorded", not "the bytes changed", and the conflict message says so.

**Why a local helper rather than a shared one.** `awr_source` has no lexical normalizer to reuse: `relative()` (`crates/awr-source/src/locator.rs:156`) is private and only *validates* that a path is relative — it returns nothing a caller could compare with. The helper added here is equality-only by construction: it is never stored, never resolves `..`, never touches the filesystem and never folds case, and no authority decision reads it. If a shared normalizer appears later, this is the single place that would switch to it.
## Tests

`crates/awr-cli/tests/execution_registry.rs`:

- `an_execution_receipt_binds_input_bytes_and_reports_drift`
- `an_interpreter_script_is_bound_from_argv_and_absence_is_explicit`
- `a_missing_input_fails_registration_when_required`
- `a_touched_input_keeps_the_key_idempotent_while_changed_bytes_conflict`
- `adding_inputs_to_an_existing_key_is_a_named_conflict`
- `content_sha256_matches_the_source_fingerprint_for_edge_sizes` - 0-byte, 1-byte and 1 MiB inputs, asserting the recorded digest equals `awr_source::fingerprint(bytes)` minus its `sha256:` prefix, plus the 64-character shape and the size.
- the documented exit code on domain failures is pinned to `1` rather than merely "not success".

`cargo fmt --all --check` exits 0. **The tests were not executed on the author's machine**: the build host hit its commit limit (`os error 1455`, page file exhausted) while linking the test binaries, so there is no local test result. CI is the authority for this head.

All five platform gates pass on `d7bb7203` - `linux-x64`, `linux-arm64`, `macos-x64`, `macos-arm64` and `windows-x64` - in native platform verification run 39252660866; the `## CI` section below is the authority for this head (16 checks, 14 success, 2 skipped, 0 failures). This change touches no file under `crates/awr-server/`.

## Change

11 files, +669/−5:

- `crates/awr-core/src/execution.rs` +119/−0
- `crates/awr-cli/src/execution.rs` +240/−2
- `crates/awr-cli/tests/execution_registry.rs` +239/−1
- `crates/awr-cli/tests/host_continuity.rs` +2/−0
- `crates/awr-cli/tests/status_action.rs` +2/−0
- `crates/awr-runtime/src/execution.rs` +2/−0

Six of these only add the new fields to existing `ExecutionIntent` literals.

The example host is a consumer of the receipt, so it has to agree with the runtime about what running a script looks like. It now:

- recomputes the interpreter script from argv with the same rule the runtime uses - the interpreter's basename without `.exe` against `python`/`python3*`/`node`/`bash`/`sh`/`zsh`/`pwsh`/`powershell`/`ruby`/`perl`, `-m`/`-c`/`-e` meaning no script, and the first non-option argument being the script;
- hashes that script **before dispatch** and keeps `script_sha256` and `script_size` on the run record, so the receipt is compared against the bytes that were on disk when the process started rather than against a file that may have been rewritten since;
- accepts exactly two shapes: `none` with an empty input list, or `argv_script` with exactly one input whose `source` is `argv_script`, whose `path` is the script it resolved and whose `sha256` and `size` equal the pre-dispatch values. A `declared` binding is still refused, because this host never passes `--bind`.

items.title: HEATR tabsq6: MF=6 capture-photon continuum weighted twice relative to discrete lines, and LEP ignored (capture damage and KERMA overstated ~20-35% for TENDL)
items.author: Connoravila1
items.body:
### Summary

In `heatr.f90` `tabsq6` (MF=6 capture photons, called from `sixbar` for MT=102), the 4-point Gauss–Legendre weights are multiplied by the full panel width `dx`. The abscissae use the half-width (`x=xl+(1+qp(j))*dx/2`), and the weights `qw` sum to 2, so each continuum panel is integrated twice over:

https://github.com/njoy/NJOY2016/blob/ab27c6414a0f25b173f2b637e6dc7e428fdaff00/src/heatr.f90#L4197-L4202

`tabdam` uses the same weights and divides by 2 (`f=f+qw(iq)*df(er,z,awr,z,awr)/2`, [heatr.f90#L2746](https://github.com/njoy/NJOY2016/blob/ab27c6414a0f25b173f2b637e6dc7e428fdaff00/src/heatr.f90#L2746)). The discrete lines are added with unit weight, so the normalisation `s` does not cancel the factor. The photon continuum is therefore counted twice relative to the discrete lines.

The routine also always interpolates the spectrum linearly (`inn=2`), whatever LEP the subsection gives.

Both affect the capture recoil damage `h` (MT=444/447) and the mean recoil energy `g` (heating, MT=301). This happens whenever an MF=6 MT=102 photon distribution has both discrete lines and a continuum, which is the case for TENDL. MF=12/15 photons go through `tabsqr`, where there are no discrete lines and the factor cancels.

The code is unchanged in 2016.80 (`main`) and on `develop`.

### Why it is wrong

[ENDF-102 (2023)](https://www.nndc.bnl.gov/endfdocs/ENDF-102-2023.pdf), §6.2 eq. (6.2) and §6.2.3:
- the LAW=1 distribution is normalised to 1;
- the first ND entries are discrete lines (delta functions, `f0` = probability);
- the rest are a continuum interpolated with LEP (1 = histogram).

TENDL-2025 Fe-56 follows this. In the first MT=102 record (E = 1e-5 eV, ND = 88, NEP = 133, LEP = 1), the discrete probabilities sum to 0.7408 and the histogram continuum integrates to 0.2592, which totals 1.0000. `tabsq6` obtains `s` = 1.234 for the same record.

### Reproduction

- Data: TENDL-2025 `n-Fe056.tendl`, sha256 `f33f867a4f9c4579a62954fe31dc6e70768ab2424dc8f282a122a93f156d2e1e`, from the official `TENDL-n.tgz` ([TENDL-2025](https://tendl.imperial.ac.uk/tendl_2025/tendl2025.html)).
- Codes: NJOY2016.79, and the same source rebuilt with the patch below.
- Deck:

```
moder
 20 -21/
reconr
 -21 -22/
 'Fe-56'/
 2631 1 0/
 0.001/
 'Fe-56'/
 0/
heatr
 -21 -22 -23/
 2631 4 0 0 0 0 40.0/
 444 445 446 447/
moder
 -23 24/
stop
```

MT=447 / MT=102 at 0.0253 eV gives the damage energy per capture:

| Target | As released | `dx/2` only | `dx/2` + LEP |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fe-56 | 214.13 eV | 141.74 eV | 160.33 eV |
| Cr-52 | 215.5 eV | | 174.1 eV |
| Ni-58 | 291.7 eV | | 240.5 eV |
| W-184 | 0.161 eV | | 0.292 eV |

The fully patched Fe-56 value, 160.33 eV, agrees with an independent adaptive integral of the record as the format specifies (160.5 eV). Fe-56 MT=301 at 0.0253 eV falls from 717.6 to 551.4 b·eV.

The patch leaves MT=445 and MT=446 bit-identical. An unpatched rebuild with the same toolchain reproduces our existing NJOY2016.79 build's MT=444–447 exactly.

### Proposed patch (against 2016.80)

```diff
@@ -2944,7 +2944,7 @@
-      call tabsq6(flo,dlo,c(iraw),law,ztt,awrt,elo,c(1))
+      call tabsq6(flo,dlo,c(iraw),law,lep,ztt,awrt,elo,c(1))
@@ -3028,7 +3028,7 @@
-      call tabsq6(fhi,dhi,c(iraw),law,ztt,awrt,ehi,c(1))
+      call tabsq6(fhi,dhi,c(iraw),law,lep,ztt,awrt,ehi,c(1))
@@ -4132,14 +4132,14 @@
-   subroutine tabsq6(g,h,a,law,z,awr,e,yld)
+   subroutine tabsq6(g,h,a,law,lep,z,awr,e,yld)
-   integer::law
+   integer::law,lep
@@ -4161,6 +4161,7 @@
    inn=2
+   if (lep.eq.1) inn=1
@@ -4197,9 +4198,9 @@
-               g=g+qw(j)*xr*dx*y
-               h=h+qw(j)*df(xr,z,awr+1,z,awr)*dx*y
-               s=s+qw(j)*dx*y
+               g=g+qw(j)*xr*dx*y/2
+               h=h+qw(j)*df(xr,z,awr+1,z,awr)*dx*y/2
+               s=s+qw(j)*dx*y/2
```

`lep` is already read from the TAB2 header in `sixbar` and passed to `getsix` in the same way.

### Related, minor

For W-184, most capture recoils lie near the 70 eV displacement threshold. The 4-point rule across the threshold is then coarse: 0.292 eV per capture with the patch, against 0.247 eV from an adaptive integral. Splitting each panel at the photon energy whose recoil equals the threshold would remove this.

items.title: Potential issue in GROUPR for photonuclear data
items.author: whaeck
items.body:
We received the an email from Tim Ware with a concern about GROUPR:

The question is whether GROUPR can handle incident photon data correctly. I think this applies equally to the NJOY99 and NJOY2012 versions of GROUPR.

Looking at the relevant code source, quantities such as the reaction threshold are scaled by (AWR+1)/AWR which makes the assumption that the incident particle is a neutron. It is not clear whether GROUPR can discriminate between incident neutrons and other incident particles.

An example which exhibits the problem is the ENDF/B-VII.0 photon data for H2, reaction is MT50. The cross section threshold in MF3 is ~2.2MeV and the Q-value about the same. However, the threshold calculated from MF6 is around 3.3MeV, due to the (1.9963+1)/1.9963 scaling factor applied.

items.title: [audit] outram-mc-libs physics/tallies: CM continuum emission clamped to the two-body bound; upstream does not clamp
items.author: theodoreOnzGit
items.body:
**What.** For CM-frame continuum emission laws the sampled CM outgoing energy is clamped to the two-body bound, `cap = E (A/(A+1))^2 + Q A/(A+1)`. Upstream applies no clamp. The cap is a two-body quantity, so applying it to multi-body channels (MT=16/17, the "other" channels with `ch.q`) can cut legitimate tail draws, and for MT=91 it piles mass exactly at the bound.

**Where.** `crates/outram-mc-libs/src/physics/scatter.rs` ~:821-828: `let cap = (e * (awr / ap1).powi(2) + q * awr / ap1).max(0.0); let e_cm_out = sampled.min(cap);` The comment justifies it by envelope scaling landing "a fraction above" the bound.

**Upstream.** `inelastic_scatter`, `src/physics.cpp:1160-1175`: samples `E_cm` from the law and transforms `E = E_cm + (E_in + 2 mu (A+1) sqrt(E_in E_cm))/(A+1)^2` with no cap.

**Why / magnitude.** A port deviation (porting rule); magnitude not measured. Two independent audit passes flagged it.

**Proposed fix.** Measure first: count `sampled > cap` over 1e6 draws for U-238 MT=91 and O-16 / Al-27 MT=16 near threshold, and histogram E' in the top bin against OpenMC. If non-negligible, remove the clamp (or restrict it to genuine two-body channels) and re-measure the ICSBEP residuals.

Part of #599.

items.title: Support --recursive flag for `awr s3 rm` and --force flag for `awr s3 rb`
items.author: GuzzoLM
items.body:
## Context

When using AWRust as a test fixture (e.g. via Testcontainers), tests typically need to tear down buckets between runs. This requires deleting all objects in a bucket and then removing it.

Currently `awr s3 rm` only deletes a single object and `awr s3 rb` fails with `BucketNotEmpty` if the bucket has objects. This makes cleanup cumbersome — you have to list and delete each object individually.

## Proposal

1. **`awr s3 rm <bucket> --recursive`** — delete all objects in the bucket (matching the AWS CLI `aws s3 rm s3://bucket --recursive` behavior)
2. **`awr s3 rb <bucket> --force`** — empty the bucket and then delete it (matching `aws s3 rb s3://bucket --force`)

## Use case

```java
// Testcontainers @AfterEach cleanup — currently requires per-object deletion
executeContainerCommand("awr s3 rb --force " + BUCKET_NAME);
```

This aligns with both the AWS CLI and MinIO's `mc rb --force` behavior, which are the two tools AWRust replaces.

## Summary

Fixes #334 (first in the #264 follow-up chain: #334 -> #335 -> #333 -> #332).

The first #264 increment emitted a UserWarning on `to_lab=True` and returned the stored CM-frame distribution unchanged. For light targets (p + He-3, p + Li, p + Be-9) this is a few-percent-wrong shape vs the physical LAB-frame angular distribution. The UserWarning documented the gap but did not fix it.

Apply the two-body elastic CM-to-LAB kinematic transform through the existing `conversion` primitives (same ones the LAW=2 handler uses):

- `compute_r2(e_in, awi=awp, awr=awr, awp=awp, q=0.0)` for the charged-particle elastic kinematic factor. For elastic Q=0 and `awi=awp`, so r^2 reduces to `(awr/awp)^2` independent of E; r > 1 for every neutron-adjacent target heavier than the proton.
- `convert_angcos_to_cmsys(mu_lab, r2)` maps the user's LAB cosines to CM cosines, one per (E, mu) query point.

The CM-frame caller broadcasts the user's mu against the E axis once; the LAB-frame caller feeds the per-E `mu_CM(mu_LAB)` map. items.title: feat(mf6): port LAW=6 (N-body phase-space) to backend-agnostic Python (issue #47)
items.author: gschnabel
items.body:
Part of issue #47 (long-term role of the Fortran extension). First PR in the easy-tier port of `endf6.f90` routines to backend-agnostic Python.

## Summary

- Replaces the Fortran-backed `mf6_get_law6` call in `get_dist2d_from_subsec_law6` with a pure-Python, backend-agnostic implementation via `primitives.array_ns` (numpy + JAX, no numba sibling needed at this scale).
- Introduces `endf_userpy/mfsec_interpretation/mf6_interpretation_subsecs_fort.py` as the Fortran-backed sibling module. Not imported by any production code path; exists only as the equivalence oracle for the new tests. Mirrors the existing `mf4_interpretation.py` / `mf4_interpretation_fort.py` split.
- `mf6_get_law6` is dropped from the Fortran imports in `_subsecs.py`. The other four Fortran routines (`mf6_get_law1`, `mf6_get_law1_disc_lines`, `mf6_get_law2`, `mf6_get_law7`) still fire; they land in follow-up PRs.

## Architecture (aligned upstream)

```
endf_userpy/mfsec_interpretation/
├── mf6_interpretation_subsecs.py         # Python (production)
├── mf6_interpretation_subsecs_fort.py    # NEW: Fortran oracle (test-only)
└── ...
```

Public signature of `get_dist2d_from_subsec_law6` gains a trailing optional `xp=None` parameter (defaults to the numpy backend) so the current `compute_dist2d_from_subsec` LAW dispatcher keeps working unchanged. Callers that want JAX pass `xp=array_ns.get_backend('jax')`.

## Physics

LAB-frame N-body phase-space, ENDF-6 manual sec. 6.2.7, following the `endf6.f90::f6law6` reference:

$$f(E, E', \mu) = C_n \cdot \sqrt{E'} \cdot (E_i^{\max} - E'_c)^{1.5\,n_{\rm psx}-4}$$

with LAB kinematic shift $E'_c = E_s + E' - 2\mu\sqrt{E_s E'}$, $E_s = (\text{AWI}\cdot\text{AWP}/(\text{AWI}+\text{AWR})^2)\,E$, and $E_i^{\max} = ((\text{APSX}-\text{AWP})/\text{APSX})\cdot((\text{AWR}/(\text{AWI}+\text{AWR}))\,E + Q)$. Normalisation constants match Fortran for $n_{\rm psx} \in \{3, 4, 5\}$; zero elsewhere (per Fortran reference).

Fully vectorised over the $(n_E, n_{E'}, n_\mu)$ outer product; zero above kinematic cutoff (`E'_c > E_i^max`) or below reaction threshold (`E_i^max <= 0`), guarded with `xp.where` so the fractional-power branch never sees a negative base.

## Tests

New `tests/test_mf6_law6_python_fortran_equivalence.py` mirrors the pattern of `test_mf4_*_python_fortran_equivalence`:

- **Bit-for-bit** equality (`rtol=1e-13`) on H-2 (n, 2n) MT=16 across a representative (E, E', mu) grid: 6 x 20 x 11 points.
- Kinematic-cutoff mask agreement: both paths return zero on the same above-threshold points.
- Physical sanity: non-negative distribution values across a broader grid.

items.title: fix(source): one boundary for authored .awr/intake sources
items.author: FreeOnePlus
items.body:
## Motivation

Takeover proposes missing goals and task ledgers as authoritative source files under `.awr/intake/` (see `docs/dev/TAKEOVER.md`). Most source writes already exempt `.awr/intake` from the runtime-owned boundary, but two problems remain:

- Sharded source writes (`crates/awr-runtime/src/source_concurrency.rs`) and organization field changes (`crates/awr-runtime/src/organization_change.rs`) still reject every path under `.awr/`, so an intake ledger behaves differently depending on which write path is used.
- The existing exemption covers the whole `.awr/intake/` directory, including files AWR writes itself (`inventory.json`, `project.toml`), and it compares paths lexically, so symlinks are not taken into account.

## Design

There is now one predicate, `awr_source::is_runtime_owned_path`, used by every source write. Everything under `.awr/` is runtime-owned **except** a path that, after resolving symlinks:

1. lies inside `.awr/intake/`,
2. is not one of `RESERVED_INTAKE_FILES` (`inventory.json`, `project.toml`), and
3. is registered as a file source in `.awr/project.toml`, or lies inside a registered directory source.

If the manifest can't be read or the path can't be resolved, the predicate fails closed and treats the path as runtime-owned.

Routed through the predicate:

- `source_concurrency.rs`: registered shard path and claimed shard path (previously raw `.awr` prefix checks).
- `organization_change.rs`: target file (previously a raw `.awr` prefix check).
- Already using it, now with the stricter rule: YAML/Markdown mutation prepare, mutation apply, work creation, batch ledger edits, content review.

**Shards: registered intake sources are allowed.** A shard target is already bound to a store-registered source of the same adapter before any journal or file write. Rejecting a registered intake source only on the sharded path would bring back the inconsistency this PR removes, with no extra safety, because the reserved runtime files and unregistered paths are still refused. The rejection messages now give the recovery step: "relocate authored documents outside .awr (except registered .awr/intake sources) and reindex".

## Compatibility

- Intake ledgers created by `init` are registered in the manifest, so existing takeover projects keep working.
- Newly refused (previously exempt): unregistered files under `.awr/intake/`, the two runtime intake files, and symlinks that resolve into runtime state. None of these are authored sources.
- No schema, migration or error-code changes; only the message text changes.

## Verification (local, Linux x64)

- `cargo build --workspace --locked`: OK
- `cargo test --workspace --locked`: 1,683 passed, 0 failed, 7 ignored, including the new `crates/awr-source/tests/intake_boundary.rs` (8 tests: registered vs unregistered intake files, reserved files even when registered, directory sources, other runtime state, symlink resolution, fail-closed manifest)
- `cargo fmt --all --check`: clean
- `python3 scripts/check_public_tree.py`: OK

## Docs

`docs/dev/TAKEOVER.md` now states the rule.

items.title: fix(source): allow work creation on authored .awr/intake ledgers
items.author: Carl-Zhou-CN
items.body:
Fixes #326

## Problem

`work create` still rejected every ledger under `.awr/` as runtime-owned while #323 already treats authored `.awr/intake/` sources as authoritative for mutation writeback and content review. A freshly initialized project (`init --accept`) therefore could not run AWR's own work lifecycle: `work create` failed with `RuleViolation: runtime files cannot be task sources`, and as the issue shows, the rejected write attempts left `approved` proposals that could never be applied.

## Change

- Use the shared `awr_source::is_runtime_owned_path` boundary in `yaml_create.rs` (work creation), so authored `.awr/intake/` ledgers are writable while every other `.awr/` path stays runtime-owned.
- Align the two remaining same-family guards that still carried the blanket `.awr/` prefix check: markdown work mutations (`markdown_mutation.rs`) and the ledger batch preflight (`ledger_batch.rs`).
- The rejection message now names the recovery (`relocate authored documents outside .awr (except .awr/intake) and reindex`), matching the mutation path wording from #323 and addressing the issue's "at least the failure tells the user what to do".

## Regression

New `intake_lifecycle` test suite:

- `intake_scaffolded_ledger_supports_the_full_work_lifecycle` — the full issue lifecycle on a scaffolded project: `init --accept` → `work create` (two-phase preview/accept) → claim → `work progress` → evidence registration → `work complete`, asserting the ledger reaches `completed`. This is the end-to-end evidence the #323 partial fix lacked.
- `runtime_owned_ledgers_still_reject_creation` — a ledger registered under `.awr/` outside `.awr/intake` is still refused with `RuleViolation`, so the authored-intake exception cannot become a prefix escape hatch. Path-escape denials keep using canonical paths via the shared boundary (also covered by the existing `security_write` suite).

items.title: Spell audit items 3 and 4: forced movement and auras reach the spells that asked
items.author: olstach
items.body:
## Forced movement — 11 of 15 spells

**The `obstacle_bonus_damage` ladder only reads as flat damage.** As a percentage, Surge's 10 would have been half a point on its 5 damage. Flat, **Surge deals 5 in the open and 15 into stone** — a level 1 nuke you have to earn by positioning. That's clearly what was meant, and the whole water ladder escalates the same idea:

| | damage | push |
|---|---|---|
| `surge` L1 | 5 | 1 tile, +10 into an obstacle |
| `wave` L3 | 10 | 1 + spellpower, +25 |
| `ripple` L5 | 15 | 2–3 tiles, +30 |
| `tsunami` L9 | 30 | 2 + heavy spellpower, +70 |

So `_apply_push` gained `blocked_damage` alongside the percentage form perks use, plus `per_spellpower`, `variance` and `direction: random` — enough for Geyser to throw people anywhere and Tsunami to sweep the field, in **one schema rather than four**. `scatter` is deliberately *not* a push: no direction, no stopping at the first obstacle.

**Four stay unwired and are recorded as such:** `jump` and `space_swap` (self-movement, position exchange), `ball_lightning` (persistent projectile), `mudra_of_touching_the_earth` (terrain destruction). Tornado keeps `persistent_effect` and `moves_randomly` for the same reason — a hazard that relocates itself each round is a system this game doesn't have, and pretending otherwise would be worse than recording it.

## Auras

Five spells declared their aura **twice** — once in `special`, once in the status that now owns it. Stale copies gone.

Radiance and Radiant Visage became real auras with carrier statuses. The four helper summons — singing birds, guiding light, apsara, gandharva host — now carry their auras on their **templates** rather than on the sentence that summoned them, which is where a creature's own behaviour belongs.

Two small generalisations that paid for themselves immediately:

- **A source may declare several auras.** Radiance both mends the allies around it *and* dazzles whoever closes to melee — different teams, different radii, not one aura.
- **`grant_status` may carry a `chance`.** The apsara's charm as a guaranteed every-turn field would end fights by itself.

Radiant Visage promised "+2 AWR and +2 CON". Those are *attributes* and an aura moves *stats*, so it grants what they'd have bought — the initiative from Awareness, the health from Constitution — and its description now says that.

## A correction to the audit

Its aura bucket was built by keyword and **mis-filed three spells**. `sunrise`, `mudra_of_touching_the_earth` and `vision_of_reality` matched on `heals_all_allies`, but they're `target: global` one-shots — battlefield instants, not standing fields. They want global targeting, and they're counted with the inert spells now. Noted in the doc.

## Verification

`verify_spells` 14 checks · 13 mutations, 13 caught
`verify_auras` 19 checks · 18 mutations, 18 caught

One aura mutation escaped first, and it was the test's fault again: the summon check set `intrinsic_auras` by hand, then asserted the template's data separately — testing both ends and not the wire between them, so unhooking the spawn path entirely left it green. It spawns through the real path now.

`tools/verify_all.sh` — `ALL CHECKS PASSED`, thirteen suites.

items.title: environment_dump false positive: boolean glosses like FALSE= and fullwidth semicolon NULL=
items.author: ngchichi
items.body:
## Summary

`awr init` rejects ordinary boolean field glosses as `category=environment_dump` / `source.public_content`. These are not environment dumps or secrets.

## Environment

- AWR 0.5.1 (`@originoneai/agent-work-runtime`)
- Windows x64

## Steps

1. Save this file as `notes.json`:

```json
[
  {"comment": "FALSE=disabled; TRUE=enabled"},
  {"comment": "状态说明；NULL=未设置"}
]
```

2. Run `awr init --goal "index public field notes"` in a directory whose source scan includes that file.

## Actual

```text
RuleViolation: rule violation: sensitive content is not accepted; remove secret values or use explicit redacted placeholders; category=environment_dump
  Rule: source.public_content
```

A decoded JSON string that starts with `FALSE=` is treated as an environment assignment. A fullwidth semicolon `；` is folded to `;`, so `；NULL=` and `；TRUE=` match the same way.

## Expected

Boolean glosses (`FALSE=`, `TRUE=`, `NULL=`) in comments should stay public. A real `export NAME=value` or an `environment:` mapping can still be rejected.

items.title: feat(locator): bind project locators when evidence is registered
items.author: shishenshashen
items.body:
## Summary

Project locator names a file relative to the project root, so one stored string resolves to the same relative path on every node that holds the checkout. Registration now resolves it exactly once through `awr_source::Locator` and stores the canonical identity; a missing or escaping target is a typed error there and never a guess at read time. A declared sha256 must match the bytes the locator resolves to.

Body reads open `project://` and nothing else: the base rejects every locator that carries a `://` scheme, this PR makes `project://` the first supported one, and `file://` and `git://` continue to be rejected. The plain-path handling, authorized-root containment and digest checks are unchanged. `evidence show` reports the locator scheme alongside the record.

`Locator::parse` no longer strips a `#L<start>[-L<end>]` selector, so a file locator with a fragment is refused at parse time again and a git locator keeps `#` as ordinary path bytes, matching the behaviour before project locators existed. Selectors stay scheme-specific: `git://` keeps `#` as ordinary path bytes, `file://` refuses any fragment, and a project locator refuses a line selector at parse time with `InvalidInput` (`project locator does not support a line selector`), because its payload is a project-relative file path in which `#` has no legal meaning.

## What changed since the review

Reviewed head: `5e32fd65`. All four points are addressed; nothing outside them moved.

### 1. One path-safety check for `project://`

`read.rs` no longer carries its own parser or containment rule. A `project://` read goes through `Locator::parse` and `Locator::read`, so syntax, the root rule and the byte read live in `awr_source::Locator` only.

The rule, stated once: a `project://` locator resolves against the project root and nothing else; `authorized_roots` does not participate. It is node-local configuration, so letting it satisfy a project locator would resolve one stored string to different bytes on another node, which is the failure this locator exists to prevent. `file://` and plain paths keep using `authorized_roots` unchanged. `Locator::parse` refuses `..`, absolute paths and every out-of-root component (`project locator must stay inside the project root`), and `Locator::read` re-checks containment after `canonicalize()`.

### 2. Project root is defined, and different bytes must fail

New section in `docs/dev/reference/workspace-exchange.md` defines the root as the canonicalized directory recorded for the project, states the one rule above, and states that a node whose file holds different bytes fails on the stored `sha256` and never falls back to another copy.

Tests:

- `crates/awr-source/tests/locator_project.rs::the_same_relative_path_with_different_bytes_never_falls_back` — two roots, same relative path, different bytes: same identity, different fingerprints, each read uses its own root.
- `crates/awr-source/tests/locator_project.rs::a_project_locator_stays_inside_the_project_root` — `..` traversal refused at parse time.
- `crates/awr-cli/tests/records_cli.rs::project_locator_read_refuses_changed_bytes_instead_of_falling_back` — end to end: bytes rewritten after registration, `evidence show --content` fails with `SourceConflict` and the project revision is unchanged.

### 3. Callers

The verifying read path is `evidence show --content`: CLI -> `Runtime::read_evidence_report` -> `read_registered_file` with the record's `sha256`. End to end:

- `crates/awr-cli/tests/records_cli.rs::project_locator_is_parsed_at_registration_and_read_back_by_show` — registration stores the canonical identity; `show --content` returns the bytes.
- `crates/awr-cli/tests/records_cli.rs::a_project_locator_that_escapes_is_refused_by_the_locator_parser` — the refusal is the parser's `RuleViolation`, which pins the single place that decides whether a project locator may leave the root.

A note on `content_hash_verified`: `evidence show --content` reports whether the record declares a `sha256`. The bytes are checked by `verify_registered_sha`; a mismatch ends the command with `SourceConflict` instead of returning content.

### 4. One registration-time check, shared with #358

#358 factors the existing containment rule out of `read_registered_file` and calls it from both the read path and the write-side guard. Its guard returns early for `project://`, so the two rules have disjoint domains and the order of the checks cannot change the outcome. This pull request adds no second registration-time check: `project://` is bound by `bind_project_locator` through `Locator`, and plain and `file://` locators keep the #358 guard. The two changes are complementary and neither duplicates the other's rule.

## What identifies the project root

A project locator stores a root-relative path; it carries no project key and no fingerprint of the root. Across nodes the declared `sha256` is the backstop: the same relative path with identical bytes is accepted, and different bytes are refused. There is no root fingerprint, so two checkouts that share a relative path are indistinguishable to the locator; that is a known limitation, and a stronger project identity is an open question in #348.

A cleanup and documentation pass. The library code under `src/` is unchanged, apart from `setup.py` packaging.

## 1. CI and packaging
- **CI never ran.** The workflow was in `.github/workflow/`, but GitHub only reads `.github/workflows/`. It is moved there and now tests Python 3.10 and 3.12.
- **`pip install -e .` installed no code.** `find_packages(where="src")` returned `[]`. `setup.py` now ships the `src` package, declares `numpy`/`h5py`, requires Python ≥ 3.10, and adds `test` and `validation` extras.
- **Five tests failed without ENDF data.** These are the cross-section tests in `test_materials_and_cross_sections.py`. They now skip when `endfb/neutron/Pb208.h5` is missing, using the same guard as the other data-dependent test files. Without data the result is 129 passed and 36 skipped.

## 2. Pruning
- **`openmc_runs/`:** removed the 27 run directories not regenerated with the current data snapshot (manifest dated 2026-08-08):
  - debug runs: `bintest`, `omc_diag`, `omc_grp`, `omc_min`, `omc_smear`, `omc_spec`, `omc_src`, `*_test`
  - cases under their old names
  - the superseded pin-cell seed and convergence sweeps

  Every run behind the current results tables is kept.
- **`Validation/`:** removed scripts that crash on the current API, because they mock a 4-value `get_cross_sections`: `validate_benchmark_point`, `validate_consistency`, `validate_reflection` and `validation_slab`. Also removed one-off data probes: `data_check` (×2), `check_angle_data`, `benchmark_speed` and `validation_physics`. The unit tests and `analytic_benchmarks.py` cover these.
- **Generated outputs:** removed both committed `dose_map.vtk` files and the scratch `Beavers_Pincell.ipynb`, which `validate_pincell.py` supersedes. `Animation/all_trajectories.json` is no longer tracked; `.gitignore` already listed it.
- **Kept:**
  - the ParaView screenshot, moved to `docs/images/mesh_tally_paraview.png`
  - `omc_pincell_seeds.json`, which was committed with the paper data
- `.gitignore` is rewritten without the dead commented rules, and there is a new `Animation/README.md`.

## 3. Documentation
`readme.md` is renamed to `README.md` and rewritten as a front page. `docs/index.md` is now the full validation report. QUICK_START and the API reference are rewritten against the actual code. Errors fixed along the way:
- **Wrong AWR.** The examples passed 207.2 (natural lead's molar mass) as Pb208's AWR, the same mix-up the validation harness was fixed for. They now use 206.190, and AWR × mₙ for the molar mass.
- **Wrong direction.** `theta=0, phi=0  # +x` actually points along +z, because `theta` is measured from +z. And `uniform(0, π)` polar angles are not isotropic.
- **Transmission always 0.** The examples read `tally.results["escaped"]`, which `merge_partial_results` never fills. They now use `tally.statistics()`.
- **Data location.** The docs said the ENDF data ships with the repo. It does not.
- **Inconsistent numbers** are reconciled with `validation_results*.csv` and `pincell_reference.json`:
  - test counts (131, 132 and 165 in different places)
  - ICSBEP and mixture z-scores
  - B10 and Fe56 χ²/dof
  - slab dimensions, which were half-thicknesses labelled as full ones
- **Stale roadmap.** It listed the vector engine and material mixtures as future work. Both exist.

New content:
- the vector-engine validation and speed-up table
- the BEAVRS pin-cell result
- worked examples for detectors, spectra, mesh tallies, trajectories, mixtures, reflective boundaries, Godiva k-eigenvalue and the vector engine
- two documented pitfalls: missing nuclide data silently gives zero cross sections, and the detector box is only tested where a neutron stops

The validation-suite README and CONTRIBUTING are updated to match.

## Verification
- `pytest` passes in a fresh virtualenv with only the `.[test]` extras: 129 passed, 36 skipped.
- A clean install imports `src` from outside the repo.
- Every Python block in `README.md`, `QUICK_START.md` and `api-reference.md` was executed against the real `CrossSectionReader`. The ENDF library couldn't be downloaded in that environment, so the runs used small synthetic OpenMC-format HDF5 files. This verifies that the API usage is correct. It does not verify physics values.
- All relative links and anchors in the markdown files resolve.

- `CrossSectionReader` returns 0 instead of raising when a nuclide file is missing.
- The element-alias map is duplicated in `cross_section_read.py`.
- `main.py`'s source uses `theta = uniform(0, π)`, which is not isotropic.
- `main_benchmark.py` and `validate_secondary.py` still pass 207.2 as Pb208's AWR.

Rewrites `skills/international/netherlands/netherlands-vat-return.md` in place (slug kept, version 2.0 to 2.1, team byline kept) for tax year 2026 in the nine-section deep-tax shape with two `oa-check` examples.
